title: The priest who gave up mirrors
translation: At the Lotus Hall of Retired Emperor Takakura there was a priest, one of the monks who chant there for the dead emperor. One day he picked up a mirror and had a long, hard look at his face. He found it so ugly and so shocking that he couldn't bear it, and even the mirror disgusted him. After that, for years, he was afraid of mirrors and wouldn't even pick one up. He stopped seeing people altogether. He came out only for the services in the hall and otherwise stayed shut in. When I heard about him, I thought, now there's someone rare.

Even people who look clever spend all their time sizing up others, and they don't know themselves. You can't know anything else if you don't know yourself. So the person who knows himself is the one who really knows something.

People don't know they're ugly. They don't know they're foolish, or that they're no good at their art, or that they don't count for much. They don't know they've got old, or that illness is closing in, or that death is near, or that they've got nowhere on the path they follow. They don't see their own faults, so of course they never hear what others say about them.

Well, your face you can see in a mirror, and your age you can count. So it's not as if you don't know. But there's nothing you can do about either, so I'd say it comes to the same as not knowing. I'm not telling you to change your face or get younger. But if you know you're bad at something, why not step back right away? If you know you're old, why not take it easy and live quietly? If you know your practice isn't getting anywhere, why not make that the one thing you think about?

Spending time with people who don't enjoy your company is embarrassing. Some people go off to serve at court, ugly and slow. They know nothing and sit with the learned, bring their second-rate skill to a room full of experts, and line up with men in their prime under a head of hair as white as snow. Worse, they want what they can't reach, fret over what won't work out, wait for what will never come, fear people and flatter them. Nobody else is shaming them. Their own greed drags them along, and they shame themselves.
And the greed never stops, because they don't really know that the one thing that matters, the end of their life, is already here.

literal: A monk of perpetual chanting at the Lotus Hall of Retired Emperor Takakura, someone called the Preceptor So-and-so, one time took a mirror and looked closely at his face, and felt so very wretched at how ugly and shocking his looks were that even the mirror seemed repellent, so afterwards for a long time he feared mirrors, did not even take one in his hand, and did not mix with people at all.
That he attended only the services in the hall and stayed shut in: when I heard this, it seemed rare and admirable.
Even clever-looking people only weigh up the affairs of others and do not know themselves.
There can be no reason by which one knows the outside without knowing oneself.
So one should call the one who knows himself a person who knows things.

Their looks are ugly but they do not know it; they do not know that their minds are foolish, do not know that their skill is clumsy, do not know that they are of no account, do not know that they have grown old, do not know that illness attacks them, do not know that death is near, do not know that the way they practise falls short; since they do not know their own faults, still less do they know the criticism from outside.
However, looks can be seen in a mirror, and age is known by counting.
It is not that one does not know one's own matters, but since there is nothing to be done, I would say it is like not knowing.
It is not that I say: change your looks and make your age young.
If you know you are clumsy, why do you not withdraw at once?
If you know you have grown old, why do you not quietly rest yourself?
If you know your practice is foolish, why is your thinking not about this?
In general, to mix with the crowd without being loved and enjoyed by people is shameful.

Going out to serve with ugly looks and a slow mind, mixing with the greatly learned while ignorant, joining the seats of the skilled with unskilled art, wearing a head of snow and lining up with people in their prime,

and still more, wishing for what one cannot reach, grieving over what cannot come true, waiting for what will not come, fearing people, flattering people: this is not shame that others give; drawn by a greedy heart, one shames oneself.
That greed does not stop is because one does not know for certain that the great matter of ending one's life has come now, here.

notes.text: A Lotus Hall ({法華堂|ほつけだう}) was a chapel for Lotus Sutra rites, often built at the grave of an emperor or noble to pray for him. This one was for Retired Emperor Takakura (1161–1181), probably at his tomb in the hills east of Kyoto.

{三昧僧|さんまいそう}: monks assigned to a hall to chant without pause for the dead. {律師|りつし}: a rank in the official Buddhist hierarchy, below {僧都|そうづ} and {僧正|そうじやう}. {何某|なにがし}: 'so-and-so'; the text does not give his name.
こそ … しか: こそ needs the realis form, so き becomes しか. ありがたし: 'rare', and so 'admirable' (see section 36).

notes.quote: 我を知らずして外を知るといふ理あるべからず
notes.text: {理|ことわり}: 'reason, principle'; the reading is the 1925 edition's. The idea that self-knowledge comes before all other knowledge is old in Chinese writing too: the Laozi says that knowing others is cleverness, knowing yourself is insight.
{数|かず}ならぬ: 'not counted', so 'of no account, unimportant'.

notes.quote: 知らぬに似たりとぞいはまし
notes.text: まし: 'I would say', a careful, hypothetical form. Kenkō grants a point here: a mirror and counting do tell you. But knowing what you cannot change, he says, comes to the same as not knowing.

notes.quote: 何ぞこれを思ふ事これにあらざる
notes.text: {何|なん}ぞ … ざる: 'why not…?', a reading of Chinese 何不. The wording is awkward ('why is your thinking not about this?'), and commentators take it as 'why not think about this above all?'
{愛楽|あいげう}: 'to love and enjoy', a Buddhist word in its Buddhist reading, given by the 1925 edition.
'Wearing a head of snow': white hair. {頭|かうべ} and {壮|さか}り are the edition's readings.

notes.quote: 命を終ふる大事今ここに来れり
notes.text: {大事|だいじ}: 'the great matter', in Buddhist writing life and death itself (compare section 59). The section starts with a priest afraid of a mirror and ends with this.
